---
title: "From Burgers to cosmology: Zel'dovich and the adhesion model"
---

## Cold matter as a sheet

Dark matter at early times is *cold*: at every position there is a single
velocity. In phase space the matter therefore occupies a thin
$d$-dimensional sheet inside the $2d$-dimensional $(\mathbf x, \mathbf v)$
space. Gravity folds and stretches this sheet, and it never tears. The
natural description is **Lagrangian**: label each fluid element by its
initial (comoving) position $\mathbf q$ and follow its trajectory

$$
\mathbf x(\mathbf q, t) = \mathbf q + \boldsymbol\Psi(\mathbf q, t).
$$ {#eq-lagrangian-map}

Mass conservation then gives the Eulerian density for free: a Lagrangian
volume element $d^dq$ is mapped to $d^dx = J\,d^dq$ with the Jacobian
$J = \det(\partial\mathbf x/\partial\mathbf q) = \det(\mathbf 1 + \nabla_q\boldsymbol\Psi)$,
so

$$
1 + \delta(\mathbf x) = \sum_{\text{streams}} \frac{1}{|J(\mathbf q_s)|},
$$ {#eq-density-jacobian}

where the sum runs over all $\mathbf q_s$ that land at $\mathbf x$
(one stream before the sheet folds, several afterwards).

## Linear theory and the choice of clock

In an expanding universe the linearized fluid equations for cold matter have
a growing solution $\delta(\mathbf x, t) = D(t)\,\delta_0(\mathbf x)$ with the
**linear growth factor** $D$. (For an Einstein–de Sitter universe $D = a$,
the scale factor; for $\Lambda$CDM it grows a little more slowly at late
times.) Everything that follows becomes simplest if we use $D$ itself as the
time variable: the equations of motion for $\mathbf x(\mathbf q, D)$ read

$$
\frac{d^2\mathbf x}{dD^2} + \frac{3}{2D}\frac{d\mathbf x}{dD} = -\frac{3}{2D^2}\nabla_{\!x}\phi,
\qquad \nabla_x^2\phi = \delta ,
$$ {#eq-eom-D}

in the EdS case (the $\Lambda$CDM corrections to the coefficients are at the
percent level and are usually absorbed into $D$). Linearizing with
$\delta = -\nabla_q\cdot\boldsymbol\Psi$ gives

$$
\boldsymbol\Psi^{(1)}(\mathbf q, D) = -D\,\nabla_q\varphi(\mathbf q),\qquad
\nabla_q^2\varphi = \delta_0 .
$$ {#eq-psi1}

## The Zel'dovich approximation is Burgers' equation

Zel'dovich [-@zeldovich1970] proposed to take the linear displacement @eq-psi1
seriously *beyond* linear theory: let each element keep moving in a straight
line with its initial velocity,

$$
\mathbf x(\mathbf q, D) = \mathbf q - D\,\nabla_q\varphi(\mathbf q).
$$ {#eq-za}

With $D$ as time the velocity $\mathbf u \equiv d\mathbf x/dD = -\nabla_q\varphi(\mathbf q)$
is constant along every trajectory. That is precisely the characteristic
solution @eq-char of the inviscid Burgers equation. In Eulerian form:

$$
\partial_D \mathbf u + (\mathbf u\cdot\nabla)\mathbf u = 0 ,
\qquad \mathbf u(\mathbf x, 0) = -\nabla\varphi(\mathbf x).
$$ {#eq-za-burgers}

The density follows from @eq-density-jacobian with
$J = \det(\mathbf 1 - D\,\nabla\nabla\varphi) = \prod_i (1 - D\lambda_i)$ in terms of
the eigenvalues $\lambda_i$ of the tidal tensor $\varphi_{,ij}$. The first
**shell crossing** happens at $D_{\rm sc} = 1/\max_{\mathbf q}\lambda_1$
along the direction of the largest eigenvalue: collapse is one-dimensional
first, producing **pancakes**, then filaments, then nodes. This is the
Burgers breaking time @eq-tstar in cosmological clothing.

::: {.callout-note title="A remarkable fact about one dimension"}
In one dimension (plane-parallel collapse) the force on a sheet depends only
on how much mass lies on either side, which does not change until sheets
cross. The Zel'dovich approximation is therefore *exact* in 1D up to shell
crossing. In more dimensions it is only the first term of the Lagrangian
perturbation series developed in the [next chapter](06-lpt.qmd).
:::

## Adhesion: switching the viscosity back on

After shell crossing the Zel'dovich sheets pass through each other and the
pancakes dissolve, whereas in reality gravity holds them together. Gurbatov,
Saichev and Shandarin [-@gurbatov1989; see also @shandarin1989; @weinberg1990;
@vergassola1994] proposed to mimic this by adding a small
viscosity to @eq-za-burgers,

$$
\partial_D \mathbf u + (\mathbf u\cdot\nabla)\mathbf u = \nu\nabla^2\mathbf u ,
\qquad \nu \to 0^+ ,
$$ {#eq-adhesion}

the **adhesion model**. Streams that would cross instead *stick*: matter
accumulates in thin shocks that are the pancakes, filaments and nodes of the
cosmic web, and the Hopf–Lax construction of @eq-hopf-lax tells us exactly
where they are. Because the flow is potential, we can solve @eq-adhesion in
closed form with the Hopf–Cole transform. With the velocity potential
$\Phi = -\varphi$ at $D = 0$,

$$
\psi(\mathbf x, D) = \int \frac{d^dq}{(4\pi\nu D)^{d/2}}
\exp\!\left[\frac{1}{2\nu}\left(\varphi(\mathbf q) - \frac{|\mathbf x-\mathbf q|^2}{2D}\right)\right],
\qquad
\mathbf u = -2\nu\nabla\ln\psi .
$$ {#eq-adhesion-hc}

The **Eulerian** velocity field at any $D$ comes out of one convolution (or
one Fourier multiplier), with no particles, no time stepping and no
shell-crossing bookkeeping. The density follows from the inverse Lagrangian
map $\mathbf q(\mathbf x) = \mathbf x - D\,\mathbf u(\mathbf x, D)$:

$$
1 + \delta(\mathbf x, D) = \det\frac{\partial\mathbf q}{\partial\mathbf x}
= \det\!\big(\mathbf 1 - D\,\nabla\nabla\Phi\big) .
$$ {#eq-density-hc}

Before shell crossing and as $\nu \to 0$ this equals the Zel'dovich density
exactly (the laboratory checks this to better than $10^{-3}$ for a plane wave).
Inside shocks $\nabla\mathbf u \sim -1/\nu$ and @eq-density-hc produces the
thin, dense walls of the adhesion model.

which the fold has become a $\delta$-function. Increase $D$ past

:::

## Hopf–Cole is a Legendre transform {#sec-legendre}

Nothing in @eq-adhesion-hc used the fact that the velocity obeys Burgers'
equation; what it used is that the Zel'dovich map is a *gradient map*,
$\mathbf x = \nabla_q\chi$ with $\chi = \tfrac12 q^2 - D\varphi(\mathbf q)$. For a
gradient map with convex $\chi$ (one stream) the inverse map is the gradient
of the Legendre transform $\chi^*(\mathbf x) = \max_{\mathbf q}[\mathbf q\cdot\mathbf x - \chi(\mathbf q)]$,
and $1 + \delta = \det\nabla\nabla\chi^*$. Writing it out,

$$
\chi^*(\mathbf x) = \tfrac12 x^2 - \min_{\mathbf q}\Big[S(\mathbf q) + \tfrac12|\mathbf x-\mathbf q|^2\Big],
\qquad S(\mathbf q) = -D\varphi(\mathbf q),
$$ {#eq-legendre}

which is the Hopf–Lax formula @eq-hopf-lax with $t = 1$ and the displacement
potential $S$ as the initial potential; the heat kernel at finite $\nu$ is its
smooth version, and Burgers' equation in $D$ is just the statement that $S$ is
linear in $D$. This suggests an obvious generalization: replace $S$ by the
longitudinal displacement potential of $n$-th order Lagrangian perturbation
theory ([Chapter 6](06-lpt.qmd)), $S_D = -D\varphi - \tfrac37 D^2\varphi^{(2)} - \dots$,
and run the same machinery. Through second order the displacement is exactly
a gradient, so this returns the *exact* 2LPT Eulerian density before shell
crossing, on the Eulerian grid and without particles. At third and fourth
order the small transverse part $\boldsymbol\Psi_T$ (about $10^{-3}$ of the
longitudinal one) breaks the gradient structure; it can be restored to first
order by correcting the inverse map, $\mathbf q(\mathbf x) \simeq \mathbf q_L(\mathbf x) - \boldsymbol\Psi_T(\mathbf q_L(\mathbf x))$.

After shell crossing the two descriptions part ways deliberately: the sheet
sums $1/|J|$ over all streams, which is the collisionless truth, while the
minimum in @eq-legendre keeps one stream per point and collects the rest in
thin walls, the adhesion model built on $n$LPT instead of Zel'dovich. The
laboratory's "Legendre lab" compares the three densities (sheet, $n$LPT
Legendre, Zel'dovich Hopf–Cole) and their power spectra side by side.

## Linear in $\psi$, nonlinear in $\delta$

Pause on what @eq-adhesion-hc says. The field $\psi = e^{\varphi/2\nu}$
evolves by *linear* diffusion, yet the density @eq-density-hc contains all
orders in $\delta_0$. Expand the determinant: at first order
$\delta \simeq D\,\nabla^2\Phi = D\,\delta_0$ (linear theory); at second order
the products of second derivatives generate the mode coupling that we will
quantify in [Chapter 7](07-mode-coupling.qmd); and the exponential in
@eq-adhesion-hc resums the whole series. Just as in one dimension, the
nonlinearity lives entirely in the exponential, the logarithm and the
determinant, while the dynamics in between is a Fourier multiplier
$e^{-\nu k^2 D}$ whose only job is to pick the right branch when streams
cross.

The approach has two shortcomings that the rest of these notes address:

* The Zel'dovich / adhesion dynamics is only the **first order** of the true
  gravitational dynamics. Higher orders, Chapter 6, add tidal and
  acceleration terms that Burgers' equation does not know about.
* The adhesion density inside shocks is not the true collapsed density;
  real pancakes have a finite thickness set by the multi-stream dynamics
  that the sheet method ([Chapter 6](06-lpt.qmd)) follows explicitly.
